description:
verify_responder_is_delegated_by (pkix-chain/src/lib.rs lines 1328-1379) hardcodes DefaultVerifier for the RFC 6960 §4.2.2.2 cryptographic delegation check:

    DefaultVerifier
        .verify_signature(
            responder.signature_algorithm.owned_to_ref(),
            issuer.tbs_certificate.subject_public_key_info.owned_to_ref(),
            &tbs_der,
            responder.signature.raw_bytes(),
        )

The rest of verify_ocsp_responder also currently hardcodes DefaultVerifier (line 1286). That itself is documented as a limitation ('callers that need a custom verifier should drop down to verify_chain'). The hardcoding becomes a real problem when the chain successfully validates under verify_chain with a custom verifier (e.g. an Ed25519- or P-521-capable backend not in DefaultVerifier) but the delegation check inside verify_ocsp_responder cannot — because it's stuck on DefaultVerifier.

SCENARIO that triggers the cost:
- Issuer CA cert uses Ed25519 (real, common in modern PKIs, RFC 8410).
- DefaultVerifier covers RSA-PKCS1v15-SHA-{256,384,512} and ECDSA-P-256-SHA-256.
- Caller validates the chain with a custom verifier that covers Ed25519 and feeds it to verify_chain. The chain validates.
- Caller wants 'and also verify this responder is delegated by issuer'. They call verify_ocsp_responder(...). The wrapper validates the chain again (now with DefaultVerifier — already a problem since the chain may fail under DefaultVerifier and the caller gets Error::Path which makes no sense given their chain was fine under the custom verifier they already proved). Then the delegation check tries Ed25519 under DefaultVerifier → no dispatch → returns Error::OcspDelegation { reason: 'signature does not verify...' } even though the responder IS legitimately delegated.

The user gets a misleading error: 'this responder isn't delegated by issuer' when in fact 'this implementation can't tell because it doesn't support Ed25519.'

MAINTENANCE CONSEQUENCE: every algorithm coverage gap in DefaultVerifier becomes a silent over-rejection in verify_ocsp_responder. The user's recourse — per the docstring at line 1326 — is to 'drop down to verify_chain and replicate the delegation check' — but the helper has no public surface, so they'd have to recreate verify_responder_is_delegated_by from scratch.

Two compounding issues with PKIX-sqek.4: both stem from the wrappers committing to DefaultVerifier without allowing the caller to pick a SignatureVerifier.

FIX: take a SignatureVerifier as a wrapper argument (same shape as Verifier::new). Pre-1.0 this is free; post-1.0 it requires an additive sibling wrapper.

This applies to ALL eight use-case wrappers, but verify_ocsp_responder is the worst case because the misleading error (Error::OcspDelegation) blames the responder rather than admitting the limitation.
title: verify_ocsp_responder hardcodes DefaultVerifier for the delegation signature binding, ignoring caller's verifier
